chandrasekhar-limit.title: Chandrasekhar Limit
chandrasekhar-limit.content:
The gravitational stability of a highly evolved stellar core that has exhausted its thermonuclear fuel depends entirely on the quantum-mechanical pressure exerted by degenerate electrons. For the dense remnants known as White Dwarfs, this outward pressure counteracts the inward pull of gravity, maintaining a stable equilibrium without requiring any thermal energy generation. The physical origin of this supportive pressure is analyzed under the framework of Electron Degeneracy Pressure, which arises from the Pauli exclusion principle as electrons are crowded into extremely high-momentum states. These degenerate stellar remnants represent one of the primary classes of dense remnants studied in astrophysics under the taxonomic family of Compact Objects, which also includes neutron stars and black holes. In the event that a white dwarf in a binary system accreted matter and exceeds its stable mass boundary, it undergoes a thermonuclear runaway explosion, generating a cosmic blast known as Type Ia Supernovae.

The maximum mass that such a degenerate stellar core can support before gravitational forces overcome the quantum-mechanical pressure is determined by the transition of the degenerate electrons into the ultra-relativistic regime. The mathematical statement of this limiting mass is given by the relativistic degeneracy mass limit relation, written as:

\[ M_{\text{Ch}} = \frac{3\sqrt{2\pi}}{8} \left( \frac{\hbar c}{G} \right)^{3/2} \left( \frac{1}{\mu_e m_H} \right)^2 \approx 1.4 M_\odot \]
where \( M_{\text{Ch}} \) represents the Chandrasekhar limit, \( \hbar \) is the reduced Planck's constant, \( c \) is the speed of light, \( G \) is the gravitational constant, \( \mu_e \) is the mean molecular weight per electron (typically equal to 2 for carbon-oxygen white dwarfs), \( m_H \) is the mass of a hydrogen atom, and \( M_\odot \) represents the solar mass. In this formulation, the limit is independent of the stellar radius, arising from a balance where both the self-gravitational pressure and the ultra-relativistic degeneracy pressure scale as the four-thirds power of the density. Consequently, if the mass of the core exceeds this mathematical threshold, no increase in density can generate sufficient pressure to halt the collapse, triggering a runaway contraction into a neutron star or black hole.

The microphysical origin of this pressure is rooted in the relativistic energy spectrum of degenerate fermions, which is governed on a microscopic scale by The Energy-Momentum Relation, relating particle energy to momentum and invariant rest mass. On an astrophysical scale, this relativistic limit is the white dwarf counterpart to the gravitational boundary that governs massive neutron stars, known as Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff Limit, which establishes the maximum mass supportable by degenerate neutrons under full general relativity. By comparing the local degeneracy pressure of stellar cores with the global gravitational expansion of the universe, astrophysicists can map the flow of energy and matter across curved spacetime manifolds, establishing the Chandrasekhar limit as a fundamental benchmark in stellar evolution. This comparison relies on modelling the white dwarf as a relativistic polytrope with index n=3, where the equation of state transitions from non-relativistic to ultra-relativistic regimes as the density climbs towards the center of the star.

The physical behavior of these degenerate stellar cores exhibits an important limiting case when the mass of the core is well below the Chandrasekhar limit. In this non-relativistic limit where \( M \ll M_{\text{Ch}} \), the Fermi momentum of the degenerate electrons remains much smaller than their rest mass energy, a regime where the electron degeneracy pressure scales as the five-thirds power of the density. Under these conditions, the stellar core is stably supported by non-relativistic degeneracy pressure, and the core's radius exhibits a stable, inverse scaling relation where the radius decreases as the mass increases, \( R \propto M^{-1/3} \). As the stellar mass increases toward the relativistic limit, the electrons are driven into the ultra-relativistic regime where their velocity approaches the speed of light \( c \). This transition is crucial for understanding how the core's behavior diverges from classical polytropic models, demonstrating how quantum degeneracy limits dictate the macroscopic fates of stars across the universe. By analyzing this transition, astronomers can model the exact boundary where a stable dwarf collapses, bridging the gap between subatomic quantum states and massive gravitational collapses in the cosmos.

jeans-mass.title: Jeans Mass
jeans-mass.content:
The fragmentation of giant molecular clouds and the subsequent initiation of star formation are governed by the balance between internal thermal pressure and self-gravitational attraction. When a gas cloud's mass exceeds a critical threshold, the inward pull of gravity overcomes the outward pressure forces, triggering a runaway gravitational collapse. The physical properties of these star-forming regions are deeply connected to the dust and gas distribution of the interstellar medium, which is observed through the absorption of starlight known as Interstellar Extinction. Over longer timescales, the stars born from this collapse evolve and develop massive mass-loss phases, which are modeled using the equations of Stellar Wind Hydro. The distance scales of these galactic structures are calibrated using standard candles, including the pulsating stars known as Cepheid Variables, which serve as the first rung of the cosmic distance ladder.

The mathematical boundary that separates stable acoustic oscillations from runaway gravitational collapse is determined by the Jeans instability criterion. The mathematical statement of this critical mass threshold is given by the Jeans mass collapse threshold relation, written as:

\[ M_J = \frac{\pi^{5/2}}{6 G^{3/2}} \frac{c_s^3}{\sqrt{\rho_0}} \]
where \( M_J \) represents the Jeans mass, \( G \) is the gravitational constant, \( c_s = \sqrt{\gamma k_B T / m} \) is the adiabatic sound speed of the gas (with \( \gamma \) being the adiabatic index, \( k_B \) being the Boltzmann constant, \( T \) being the temperature, and \( m \) being the mean molecular mass), and \( \rho_0 \) represents the unperturbed background mass density of the gas cloud. In this formulation, the Jeans mass scales as the cube of the sound speed and is inversely proportional to the square root of the density. This means that hotter, less dense gas clouds require a much larger mass to initiate collapse, whereas cold, dense regions can easily fragment into smaller, stellar-sized cores.

The microphysical propagation of energy and momentum within these collapsing gas clouds is constrained by the relativistic energy spectrum of the gas particles, which is governed by The Energy-Momentum Relation, relating particle energy to momentum and invariant rest mass. On a cosmological scale, these local collapse dynamics occurred within the expanding background of the early universe, a process historically modeled by The Einstein-de Sitter Universe (\(\Omega_m = 1\)), which describes a flat, matter-dominated universe with zero cosmological constant. In this expanding matter-dominated background, the growth rate of density perturbations is suppressed from exponential to power-law growth, demonstrating how the global cosmic expansion rate counteracts the local self-gravitational instability.

The mathematical derivation of this instability is performed by linearizing the fundamental fluid equations—the continuity equation, the Euler equation, and the Poisson equation for gravity—about a uniform background state. To solve these differential equations, physicists must specify appropriate physical constraints at the cloud's edges, which are defined as the Boundary Conditions of the system. By introducing small density perturbations of the form \( \delta \rho \propto e^{i(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x} - \omega t)} \), physicists can derive a dispersion relation that relates the perturbation frequency to the wavevector. This dispersion relation reveals that if the perturbation wavelength exceeds the Jeans length, the frequency becomes imaginary, transforming the stable acoustic wave into an exponentially growing mode that drives runaway gravitational collapse.

In the modern cosmological epoch, this gravitational instability is analyzed within a multi-component universe where the global expansion rate is dominated by dark energy, which also drives the accelerated expansion of the cosmic scale factor. This expansion freezes out the growth of large-scale structure, preventing the formation of new galaxy clusters. Consequently, the Jeans mass in the intergalactic medium increases rapidly, demonstrating how the global dark energy density alters the local collapse thresholds of baryonic matter across cosmological timescales.

The physical behavior of these gaseous perturbations exhibits an important limiting case when the mass of the gas cloud is much smaller than the Jeans mass. In this small-scale limit where \( M \ll M_J \), or equivalently when the perturbation wavelength is much shorter than the Jeans length \( \lambda \ll \lambda_J \), the thermal pressure forces within the gas dominate over the self-gravitational attraction. Under these high-pressure conditions, the self-gravitational term in the dispersion relation becomes completely negligible, and the density perturbation propagates harmlessly through the medium as a stable acoustic wave traveling at the sound speed \( c_s \). As the gas cloud cools, the sound speed decreases, causing the Jeans mass to drop until the cloud's mass exceeds the threshold, triggering the transition from stable wave propagation to gravitational collapse. This dynamic transition explains how diffuse cosmic gas eventually condenses into the dense stellar structures that illuminate the modern universe.
